pronunciation.note: Tártaros is Tier 2 because the Greek Τάρταρος preserves only stress (acute on the first alpha), not length. The first syllable carries the pitch peak, appropriate for a name that denotes the deepest point of the cosmos. The absence of long vowels makes the name sound hard and abrupt — the acoustic opposite of the bright, sustained Aithḗr.

domains.title: The Primordial Abyss
domains.lead: Tártaros is the deepest place. It lies beneath Hades as far as Hades lies beneath the earth, and the earth beneath the sky. It is not merely a dungeon; it is a cosmic depth, the inverted dome that balances the celestial dome above.

mythology.lead: Tártaros appears almost as soon as the world begins. It is the third primordial in Hesiod's list — gap, earth, abyss — and it remains the final destination for every cosmic rebel, from the Titans to the greatest of mortal sinners.

myths.title: The Third Primordial
myths.text: When the world began, Hesiod names three things that came to be of themselves: Cháos, the yawning gap; Gaia, the broad-breasted earth; and 'dim Tártaros, in the depths of the broad-pathed earth' (Theogony 116–120). The name may be older than Greek itself: a Linear B tablet from Knossos (Fp 14) appears to pair an offering 'to Tartaro' with offerings to the gods. Homer adds the famous measurement: Tártaros lies as far beneath Hades as heaven is above earth, and a brazen anvil would fall nine days and nine nights before striking bottom (Iliad 8.13–16). The same passage sets the house of Hades at the edge of that vertical map, with Tártaros the deepest landmark on it. The myth gives the cosmos two domes — the bright one above and the dark one below — and Tártaros is the floor of everything.

myths.title: The Titans Cast Down
myths.text: When the ten-year Titanomachy ended, Zeus hurled the defeated Titans down 'under the murky gloom of the misty darkness' — into Tártaros, where a bronze fence runs round it, Poseidon fixed gates of bronze, and the Hundred-Handers stand as guards 'beyond the gates, the faithful wardens' (Hesiod, Theogony 713–735). The Iliad gives the scene from below: there the Titans sit at the threshold, 'a dreadful thing to hear' for any who would approach (Iliad 8.478–481). The terror is acoustic as much as visual — the passage stresses the sound that rises from below the threshold. Imprisonment rather than destruction is the telling detail — the old powers cannot be unmade, only stored, and the world's stability depends on their continued confinement. Tártaros is less a dungeon than a vault: the deep holds what heaven cannot afford to have loose.

myths.title: Tartarus and Gaia
myths.text: Angered by the destruction of her children the Giants, Gaia lay with Tártaros and bore Typhōn, 'youngest of her children... a bane to mortals' (Hesiod, Theogony 820–822; cf. Apollodorus, Library 1.6.1–3). He was a thing of a hundred serpent heads, fire glaring from his eyes, voices like gods and bulls and lions and hounds; he fought Zeus for the cosmos and very nearly won, until the father of gods closed with him on Mount Aitne and burned the monster's heads with thunderbolts, flinging the trunk into Tártaros — or, in the other tradition, under Aitne itself, whose eruptions are Typhōn's breath. The genealogy is the point: when Gaia needs a weapon against heaven, she mates with the deep. Tártaros is not only the prison of the old gods; it is generative — the chthonic partner through which earth produces what heaven most fears.

myths.title: Sisyphus, Tantalus, Ixion
myths.text: In later tradition Tártaros became the place of punishment for the greatest sinners among mortals. Plato's Gorgias (523a–526d), mythologizing an underworld judgment, sends the incurable down to Tártaros itself, whence they never emerge. The canonical residents were known to every Greek: Sisyphus, who rolls his boulder forever up the hill; Tantalus, chin-deep in water he cannot drink, beneath fruit he cannot reach; Ixion, bound to a blazing wheel for his treachery to Zeus; Tityos, whose liver the vultures renew daily (Homer, Odyssey 11.576–600; Virgil, Aeneid 6.580–627). These images of eternal, futile labour shaped Jewish and Christian hell at second hand, and through them the whole Western imagination of damnation. Their power lies in the punishments' precision: each torment is the crime made perpetual. Plato adds that the judges themselves — Minos, Rhadamanthys, Aiakos — hold court at the divide and cast the incurable downward (Gorgias 523e–524a).

lore.syncretism: The Romans transliterated the name directly as Tartarus and made it the lowest region of the underworld, a place of torment distinct from the neutral infernum. In Virgil's Aeneid, the wicked are judged and cast into Tartarus, while the blessed ascend to Elysium. Christian writers — above all Milton in Paradise Lost — adopted Tartarus as a name for Hell or its precinct, completing a transformation from cosmic depth to moral prison. The word remains in theological vocabulary as a synonym for the deepest place of punishment, and 2 Peter 2:4 borrows the Greek name for the prison of the fallen angels.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tártaros survives as the archetype of the inescapable prison. Video games, fantasy novels, and comic books use 'Tartarus' for the deepest dungeon, the final level, the place where ancient evils are chained. In astronomy, the exoplanet HD 80606 b was nicknamed 'Tartarus' for its extreme, hellish orbit. The abyss also shaped psychology and literature: the 'Tartarus' within is the unconscious depth where repressed forces rage. The name still carries its original weight: not merely death, but the bottom of everything.
lore.extendedMeditation:
There is a depth beneath death, and the Greeks named it Tártaros. It is not hell in the modern sense, because it holds gods as well as sinners — the Titans, Typhōn, and the most monstrous hybrids of earth and abyss. It is the cosmic landfill, the place where order stores what it cannot destroy but dare not release.

Every culture has such a place: a pit, a dungeon, a black hole. Tártaros is the Greek version, measured with Homeric precision and built with bronze. To restore the accent on the first syllable is to hear the name as a falling thing — the sound of a stone dropped into a well so deep that it falls for nine days before it hits bottom.
lore.archaeology: Tartaros has no independent cult, but its cosmography appears in texts and images. The Derveni Papyrus (ca. 340 BCE) discusses the underworld prison of the Titans. The Gigantomachy on the Pergamon Altar and the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi depict Zeus hurling enemies into Tartaros. Volcanic regions, especially Mount Etna, were later identified as mouths of Tartaros. A Linear B tablet from Knossos (Fp 14) may already attest the divine name in the second millennium BCE.
